advances: Proves the requested exponential rank surplus for the second reflection moment under the original uniform root law on every two-resource positive-coefficient downset. The auxiliary product law estimates the entire unweighted numerator of that original moment. No change of the root law or selection of one good center is substituted for the required average.
author: research-agent
external_sources: None. The sole accepted input is the one-coordinate geometric reflection-moment inequality (1) from `609407d6db81b18b`, with the explicit normalization map stated above. The multiplier selection, truncation at \(s=\log3\), simultaneous margins, and original-law average comparison are proved here.
proof:
The set \(D\) is finite, nonempty, and contains zero. It is complete: its defining real resource polytope contains \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\), so every lattice point of \(\operatorname{conv}(D)\) satisfies the defining inequalities and belongs to \(D\). If \(R=0\) or \(T=0\), positivity of the corresponding coefficients gives \(D=\{0\}\), and the left side is one. Since \(0<a<1\) and \(1<g<4\), this proves the assertion in these cases. Assume henceforth that \(R,T>0\).

We first record elementary coordinate estimates. For \(s>0\), use \(\rho=e^{-s}\), write \(\mu(s)=\mathbb E_{Q_{e^{-s}}}k\), and retain the exact \(F,Q_\rho,L(\rho)\) from the statement. Accepted fact `609407d6db81b18b` proves
\[
L(\rho)\ge\frac8{27}\qquad(0<\rho<1).
\tag{1}
\]
The following additional bounds will be proved here:
\[
\mu(s)\le\frac2s,\qquad
\mathbb E_{Q_{e^{-s}}}k^2\le\frac7{s^2}\quad(s>0),\qquad
\mu(s)\ge\frac1{10s}\quad(0<s\le\log3).
\tag{2}
\]
Put \(z=e^{-3s}\). The probability generating function \(F(zt)/F(z)\) factors as
\[
\frac{1+6zt+z^2t^2}{1+6z+z^2}
\left(\frac{1-z}{1-zt}\right)^3.
\]
Thus a variable with law \(Q_{e^{-s}}\) is a sum of independent variables: three geometric variables with masses \((1-z)z^k\), and a variable \(K\in\{0,1,2\}\) with probabilities proportional to \(1,6z,z^2\). If \(Y\) denotes the sum of the three geometric variables, then
\[
\mathbb EY=\frac{3}{e^{3s}-1}\le\frac1s,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}Y=\frac{3z}{(1-z)^2}\le\frac1{3s^2},\qquad
\mathbb EY^2\le\frac4{3s^2}.
\]
The variance estimate follows from \(z/(1-z)^2=(4\sinh^2(3s/2))^{-1}\) and \(\sinh u\ge u\). Also \(\mathbb EK\le8e^{-3s}\) and \(\mathbb EK^2\le10e^{-3s}\). The maxima of \(s e^{-3s}\) and \(s^2e^{-3s}\) are \(1/(3e)\) and \(4/(9e^2)\), respectively. Using \(e>8/3\) gives \(\mathbb EK\le1/s\) and \(\mathbb EK^2\le1/s^2\). Hence \(\mu(s)\le2/s\), and
\(\mathbb E(Y+K)^2\le2\mathbb EY^2+2\mathbb EK^2\le14/(3s^2)<7/s^2\).
Finally \(u/(e^u-1)\) decreases for \(u>0\), so for \(s\le\log3\),
\[
s\mu(s)\ge\frac{3s}{e^{3s}-1}
\ge\frac{3\log3}{26}>\frac1{10}.
\]
This proves (2).

We choose the resource multipliers using a truncated convex potential. Put \(h=\log3\),
\[
\psi(s)=\tfrac13\log F(e^{-3s}),\qquad
\phi(s)=\max\{0,\psi(s)-\psi(h)\}\quad(s>0),\qquad \phi(0)=+\infty.
\]
The function \(\psi\) is convex and strictly decreasing, with derivative \(\psi'(s)=-\mu(s)\). Indeed it is one third of the logarithm of a sum of exponentials, and differentiation gives the displayed expectation; its second derivative is three times the positive coordinate variance. Thus \(\phi\) is convex, vanishes for \(s\ge h\), and diverges as \(s\downarrow0\).
Minimize on the nonnegative quadrant
\[
\mathcal F(\lambda,\eta)=\lambda R+\eta T+
\sum_{i=1}^n\phi(\lambda b_i+\eta c_i).
\tag{3}
\]
There is a finite minimizer. The value at \((1,0)\) is finite, and \(\mathcal F\ge\lambda R+\eta T\), so a finite sublevel is bounded. A minimizing subsequence converges in the closed quadrant. Divergence of \(\phi\) at zero excludes any zero coordinate argument at the limit, and continuity at the resulting positive arguments proves attainment. Fix a minimizer and write
\(s_i=\lambda b_i+\eta c_i>0\), \(\mu_i=\mu(s_i)\), and \(\Lambda=\lambda R+\eta T\).
In particular, the multipliers cannot both vanish. No coordinate law with \(s_i=0\) is used.

There exists a vector \(x\) with
\[
x_i=\mu_i\ (s_i<h),\qquad x_i=0\ (s_i>h),\qquad
0\le x_i\le\mu_i\ (s_i=h),
\]
such that
\[
b\cdot x\le R,\qquad c\cdot x\le T,
\qquad \lambda(R-b\cdot x)=\eta(T-c\cdot x)=0.
\tag{4}
\]
Here is a justification that includes zero multipliers. Let \(\mathcal X\) be the box described above and let
\(G=\{(R-b\cdot x,T-c\cdot x):x\in\mathcal X\}\).
Let \(\mathcal Q\) be the cone whose first coordinate is zero if \(\lambda>0\), and nonnegative if \(\lambda=0\), and whose second coordinate has the corresponding rule for \(\eta\). If \(G\) and \(\mathcal Q\) were disjoint, take a nearest pair \(g_0,u_0\) and set \(v=u_0-g_0\ne0\). Compactness of \(G\) and closedness of \(\mathcal Q\) ensure existence and positive distance. Minimizing distance along segments gives \(v\cdot g\le v\cdot g_0\) for \(g\in G\) and \(v\cdot u\ge v\cdot u_0\) for \(u\in\mathcal Q\). Since \(\mathcal Q\) is a cone, its latter inequality implies \(v\cdot u_0=0\), and therefore
\(\max_{g\in G}v\cdot g\le-\|v\|^2<0\).
It also gives \(v_1\ge0\) when \(\lambda=0\), and \(v_2\ge0\) when \(\eta=0\), so \(v\) is a feasible direction at the minimizer. The directional derivative of (3) in this direction is exactly \(\max_{g\in G}v\cdot g\): at \(s_i=h\), the directional derivative of \(\phi\) is the maximum of zero and \(-\mu_i(v_1b_i+v_2c_i)\); away from a tie it is the ordinary derivative. A strictly negative derivative contradicts minimality. Hence \(G\cap\mathcal Q\ne\varnothing\), which is (4).

Choose an extreme point of the nonempty compact polytope in (4), imposing the first resource as an equality when \(\lambda>0\) and the second when \(\eta>0\). At most two tied coordinates satisfy \(0<x_i<\mu_i\). Otherwise a nonzero vector supported on three such coordinates and orthogonal to both \(b,c\) would permit small perturbations in both directions, preserving both sums and the box. This contradicts extremality. Define
\[
I_0=\{i:x_i=\mu_i\},\qquad I_* =\{i:0<x_i<\mu_i\}.
\]
Then \(|I_*|\le2\), every \(i\in I_0\) has \(s_i\le h\), and every \(i\notin I_0\) has \(s_i\ge h\). From (4),
\[
\Lambda=\sum_i s_i x_i,\qquad
\sum_{i\in I_0}b_i\mu_i\le R,\qquad
\sum_{i\in I_0}c_i\mu_i\le T,\qquad
\sum_{i\in I_*}s_ix_i\le4.
\tag{5}
\]
The last inequality uses \(s_i\mu_i\le2\) from (2).

We now create both variance margins by changing at most \(O(\sqrt n)\) coordinate rates. If \(I_0\ne\varnothing\), put
\(k=\min\{|I_0|,\lceil\kappa\sqrt n\rceil\}\).
Choose \(I_b,I_c\subset I_0\), each of cardinality \(k\), consisting respectively of the largest \(b_i\mu_i\) and \(c_i\mu_i\), with arbitrary tie resolution, and set \(I=I_b\cup I_c\). If \(I_0=\varnothing\), set \(I=\varnothing\). In every case
\[
|I|\le2\kappa\sqrt n+2.
\tag{6}
\]
Let \(J_i\), \(i\in I_0\), be independent with law \(Q_{e^{-s_i'}}\), where \(s_i'=\kappa s_i\) for \(i\in I\), and \(s_i'=s_i\) otherwise. For \(i\notin I_0\), set \(J_i=0\) deterministically. Denote this auxiliary product law by \(\mathbb P_Q\), and put \(\nu_i=\mathbb E_QJ_i\) for \(i\in I_0\). Equations (2) imply
\[
\nu_i\le\frac{20}{\kappa}\mu_i\le\frac14\mu_i\quad(i\in I),\qquad
\mathbb E_QJ_i^2\le\frac7{(s_i')^2}.
\tag{7}
\]
For \(r=b,c\), define, at any nonnegative integer vector \(j\),
\(\sigma_r(j)^2=\sum_i r_i^2j_i(j_i+1)/3\).
When \(I_0\ne\varnothing\), put \(U_r=\sum_{i\in I_r}r_i\mu_i>0\). By (7),
\[
\mathbb E_Q(r\cdot J)
\le\sum_{i\in I_0}r_i\mu_i-\tfrac34 U_r.
\tag{8}
\]
Since \(\mu_i\ge1/(10s_i)\) on \(I_0\), the coordinate second-moment estimates show that both
\(\operatorname{Var}_Q(r\cdot J)\) and \(\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2\) are at most
\[
700\sum_{i\in I_0}\frac{(r_i\mu_i)^2}{(s_i'/s_i)^2}
\le700\bigl(\kappa^{-2}+\kappa^{-2}\bigr)U_r^2
\le\frac{U_r^2}{48^2}.
\tag{9}
\]
To verify the middle inequality, the sum over \(I_r\) is at most \(U_r^2/\kappa^2\). If \(k<|I_0|\), every other \(r_i\mu_i\le U_r/k\), so the remaining sum is at most \(nU_r^2/k^2\le U_r^2/\kappa^2\). If \(k=|I_0|\), that remaining sum is zero. Shrinking coordinates in \(I\setminus I_r\) only improves the estimate. The bound for \(\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2\) uses the integer inequality \(J_i(J_i+1)\le2J_i^2\), so its coordinate coefficient \(1400/3\) is no larger than 700. The last inequality in (9) is the exact numerical comparison \(1400\cdot48^2\le4096^2\).

The dual loss and its variance satisfy
\[
\begin{aligned}
0\le\Lambda-\mathbb E_Q(s\cdot J)
&\le4+2|I|,\\
\operatorname{Var}_Q(s\cdot J)&\le7n.
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
For the first line, use (5), the dropped indices \(I_*\), and \(s_i(\mu_i-\nu_i)\le s_i\mu_i\le2\) for each \(i\in I\). The second follows by independence and \(s_i^2\mathbb E_QJ_i^2\le7\).

Consider the event on which, for each \(r=b,c\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
|r\cdot J-\mathbb E_Q(r\cdot J)|
&\le4\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_Q(r\cdot J)},\\
\sigma_r(J)&\le4\sqrt{\mathbb E_Q\sigma_r(J)^2},\\
s\cdot J&\ge\mathbb E_Q(s\cdot J)-4\sqrt{7n}.
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
\]
The final inequality is one event, not a separate condition for each resource. Chebyshev's inequality for the two resource sums and the dual sum, Markov's inequality for the two squared \(\sigma_r\)'s, and a union bound give probability at least \(1-5/16\ge1/2\). Any zero-variance or zero-expectation condition holds identically and has no exceptional event. If \(I_0=\varnothing\), \(J=0\) and all these conditions hold identically.
On this event, (5), (8), and (9) imply
\[
b\cdot J+2\sigma_b(J)\le R,\qquad
c\cdot J+2\sigma_c(J)\le T.
\tag{12}
\]
Indeed, for either resource, the increase above the expectation in (8) plus twice the allowed \(\sigma_r\) is at most \(4U_r/48+8U_r/48=U_r/4\), smaller than the reserved \(3U_r/4\). The assertion is immediate when \(I_0=\varnothing\). Equations (10) and (11) also give
\[
s\cdot J\ge\Lambda-D_n,\qquad
D_n=4+2|I|+4\sqrt{7n}.
\tag{13}
\]

At any \(j\) satisfying (12), let \(V_i\) be independent and uniform on \(\{-j_i,\ldots,j_i\}\). The two resource sums have mean zero and variances \(\sigma_b(j)^2,\sigma_c(j)^2\). Chebyshev's inequality and a union bound give probability at least \(1/2\) that \(|b\cdot V|\le2\sigma_b(j)\) and \(|c\cdot V|\le2\sigma_c(j)\). The zero-variance cases again hold identically. The endpoints \(j\pm V\) are nonnegative, and (12) puts both in \(D\). Therefore
\[
k_j\ge\tfrac12\prod_i(2j_i+1).
\tag{14}
\]

It remains to compare the entire original moment. Nonnegative multipliers imply the original partition upper bound
\[
N_D\le e^\Lambda\prod_{i=1}^n(1-e^{-s_i})^{-1}.
\tag{15}
\]
Indeed, for \(z\in D\), \(s\cdot z\le\Lambda\), so \(1\le e^\Lambda e^{-s\cdot z}\); summing and extending to the orthant proves (15).
Put \(Z_Q=\prod_{i\in I_0}F(e^{-3s_i'})\), with an empty product equal to one. For every vector in the support of the auxiliary law,
\[
\prod_i(2j_i+1)^2=Z_Q\mathbb P_Q(J=j)e^{3\sum_{i\in I_0}s_i'j_i}
\ge Z_Q\mathbb P_Q(J=j)e^{3s\cdot j}.
\]
Sum (14) squared over the event (11), which has auxiliary probability at least \(1/2\) and consists of original roots in \(D\). Use (13) and (15) to obtain
\[
\frac{\sum_{j\in D}k_j^2}{N_D^3}
\ge\tfrac18 e^{-3D_n}Z_Q\prod_i(1-e^{-s_i})^3.
\tag{16}
\]
This is a lower bound for the original uniform average, with its original normalizing denominator \(N_D^3\).

For \(i\in I_0\setminus I\), the coordinate factor in (16) is \(L(e^{-s_i})\ge8/27\) by (1). For \(i\notin I_0\), \(s_i\ge\log3\), so its factor is \((1-e^{-s_i})^3\ge8/27\). For \(i\in I\),
\[
\frac{F(e^{-3\kappa s_i})}{F(e^{-3s_i})}\ge\frac1{8\kappa^3}.
\tag{17}
\]
The numerators \(1+6z+z^2\) of \(F(z)\) lie between 1 and 8 on \(0\le z\le1\), and \(1-e^{-\kappa t}\le\kappa(1-e^{-t})\) for integer \(\kappa\ge1\), by the geometric-sum identity. These prove (17). Thus (1), (16), and (17) yield
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{j\sim p}\mathsf H_j^2
&\ge\tfrac18 e^{-12-6|I|-12\sqrt{7n}}
(8\kappa^3)^{-|I|}(8/27)^n\\
&\ge e^{-C_0-C_1\sqrt n}(8/27)^n,
\end{aligned}
\tag{18}
\]
where the second line is (6) and the constants in the statement.
Finally \(8/27=(32/27)/4=e^{2\delta}/4\), and completing the square gives
\(\delta n-C_1\sqrt n\ge-C_1^2/(4\delta)\).
Consequently (18) is at least
\(\exp(-C_0-C_1^2/(4\delta))e^{\delta n}4^{-n}=a g^n4^{-n}\).
This proves the uniform claim, including an inactive resource multiplier, tied coordinates, an empty random-coordinate set, and every zero-resource case.
statement:
Let \(n\ge1\) be an integer, let \(b_i,c_i>0\) for \(1\le i\le n\), and let \(R,T\ge0\). Thus the conclusion includes positive integer resource coefficients. Put
\[
D=\{z\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^n:b\cdot z\le R,\ c\cdot z\le T\},\qquad
N_D=|D|,\qquad p(j)=N_D^{-1}\quad(j\in D).
\]
For \(j\in D\), define the oriented reflected count, including zero displacement, and its normalized overlap by
\[
k_j=\#\{v\in\mathbb Z^n:j+v,j-v\in D\},\qquad
\mathsf H_j=\frac{k_j}{N_D}.
\]
Equivalently, this is the reflected Hellinger mass \(\sum_v\sqrt{p(j+v)p(j-v)}\) for the zero-extended uniform law. There are absolute constants \(a>0\) and \(g>1\), independent of all these data, such that
\[
\mathbb E_{j\sim p}\mathsf H_j^2
=\frac{\sum_{j\in D}k_j^2}{N_D^3}
\ge a g^n4^{-n}.
\]
One explicit choice is as follows. Set
\[
\begin{aligned}
\kappa&=4096,& B&=6+\log(8\kappa^3),\\
C_0&=\log8+12+2B,& C_1&=2\kappa B+12\sqrt7,\\
\delta&=\tfrac12\log(32/27),&
g&=e^\delta,& a&=\exp\left(-C_0-\frac{C_1^2}{4\delta}\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
All logarithms are natural. The generating function \(F\), geometric parameter \(\rho\), product-coordinate law \(Q_\rho\), and one-coordinate moment \(L(\rho)\) used below have exactly the normalization of accepted fact `609407d6db81b18b`: \(F(z)=(1+6z+z^2)/(1-z)^3\), \(Q_\rho(k)=(2k+1)^2\rho^{3k}/F(\rho^3)\), and \(L(\rho)=(1-\rho)^3F(\rho^3)\). The present reflected count is on \(D\), rather than on the composition slice in that predecessor.
